idiom_name: interface (or object type) declaration - erased at runtime, checked structurally
implementation_notes: TypeScript's interface (or an equivalent object type) names a structural contract and disappears before the JavaScript runs, so the contract can hold neither state nor behaviour and a class satisfies it by shape; implements documents the intent and makes the compiler check the implementation at the declaration site. What the erased form cannot do is exist at run time, so the classic abstract class is still the tool when the contract needs runtime presence - private or protected enforcement, instanceof, shared default behaviour - and declaration merging lets the module that owns an implementation extend the contract it satisfies. Prefer the erased interface for dependency and data shapes and reach for the abstract class only when something must happen at run time.
pitfalls: The contract is erased, so it validates nothing at run time: incoming JSON still needs a schema guard, and typing the parsed object as Reader proves only that the author said so.
Structural typing cuts both ways: any compatible object is accepted, and a class can stop matching the interface without an error until it is actually assigned to that type.

An interface that extends a class with private or protected members can be implemented only by that class's subclasses, and declaration merging lets a dependency's contract grow behind your back - a conflicting member is an error, a compatible one silently widens it.
